title: Availability Heuristic
description: We judge how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, or emotional events hijack our frequency estimates.
shortDescription: We judge how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, or emotional events hijack our frequency estimates.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We judge how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, or emotional events hijack our frequency estimates.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: After seeing a plane crash on the news, you feel flying is dangerous, even though it’s statistically safer than driving.
A manager overestimates the number of employees slacking off because one dramatic firing stands out in memory.
You assume crime is rising because you can recall several local incidents, even if statistics show a decline.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Making decisions based on the most memorable anecdote, not data.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “You hear about it all the time.” (when it’s actually rare)
“I know someone who…” (as evidence for a trend)
“Better safe than sorry” (when sorry is a vivid but improbable disaster).

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Your risk perception swings sharply after a single news story.
You can easily picture the bad outcome but struggle to recall the many uneventful cases.
You dismiss statistics in favor of “real stories.”

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The brain takes cognitive shortcuts. Easily recalled examples feel frequent, and emotionally charged memories (fear, shock) are stickier. This helped ancestors avoid rare but deadly threats.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
sections.content: When assessing likelihood, ask: “What does the base rate say?” and “How many uneventful cases am I ignoring?” Deliberately look up data rather than relying on memory.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking you’re immune because you know statistics. The bias operates automatically; you must actively counter it.
Using availability to argue against valid precautions just because the bad thing is rare.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A parent refuses to let their child walk to school alone because they vividly remember a kidnapping case from ten years ago. They ignore that the real statistical danger—car accidents—is something they engage with daily without a thought.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The ease with which a fear comes to mind is not a measure of its likelihood. Your memory is a highlight reel, not an actuarial table.
